issues.body:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-09-centrifuge/blob/512e7a71ebd9ae76384f837204216f26380c9f91/src/PoolManager.sol#L149-L163
https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-09-centrifuge/blob/512e7a71ebd9ae76384f837204216f26380c9f91/src/PoolManager.sol#L136-L147


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
User can call `transferTrancheTokensToCentrifuge` or `transferTrancheTokensToEVM` to transfer their tranche tokens to other chains, but no verifying is done to see if they are expired members or not on the source chain, which can cause loss of funds for some users.

## Proof of Concept
The function `handleTransferTrancheTokens` that is called on the destination chain is verifying if the receiver address is a expired or active member 
https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-09-centrifuge/blob/512e7a71ebd9ae76384f837204216f26380c9f91/src/PoolManager.sol#L272-L275
but no checks are done on the source chain when the transfer is made 
https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-09-centrifuge/blob/512e7a71ebd9ae76384f837204216f26380c9f91/src/PoolManager.sol#L136-L147
https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-09-centrifuge/blob/512e7a71ebd9ae76384f837204216f26380c9f91/src/PoolManager.sol#L149-L163
which can lead to loss of funds for a user which membership has expired and he doesn't know. Since the member system is time-based, users can get expired and still call `transferTrancheTokensToCentrifuge` or `transferTrancheTokensToEVM` which will burn their tokens, but the transfer will be blocked on the destination chain, causing loss of funds for the users.

## Tools Used
Manual review
## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Consider checking for active members in the source chain transfer functions also to mitigate the loss of funds for the users.

issues.title: requestDeposit and requestRedeem do not allow for any price guarantee, opening users to sandwich attacks and other losses

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-09-centrifuge/blob/512e7a71ebd9ae76384f837204216f26380c9f91/src/LiquidityPool.sol#L214-L217
https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-09-centrifuge/blob/512e7a71ebd9ae76384f837204216f26380c9f91/src/LiquidityPool.sol#L231-L234


# Vulnerability details

## Impact

Request functions take only the desired input amount as a parameter, giving no way for the caller to control the fulfilment price. The price is decided by the Centrifuge mainnet only.
```
    function requestDeposit(uint256 assets, address owner);
    function requestRedeem(uint256 shares, address owner); 
```

If there is anyway for an attacker to affect the price, eg. front running the request, manipulating an oracle used by Centrifuge or if the transaction get’s delayed users will be loosing funds.

Given the asynchronous nature of the system and it’s reliance on 3rd party bridges there are many scenarios in which a significant delay may happen for example:
- bridge outage
- tx getting priced out
- insufficient liquidity on Centrifuge
- other

I'd like to reiterate that is a potential loss that cannot be prevented by the user and which is also largely not controlled by the protocol. Furthermore it is not following the de facto DEFI standard. 

Note on severity: It could be argued that users using the platform will implicitly agree to this risk, on the other side it is highly likel that many users will be simply chose not to use it. I would argue that 
it would render the protocol largely unuseable.

## Tools Used
Manual review.
## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Add `minAmountOut` and `deadline` in the requestDeposit and requestRedeem  as well as downstream from them, including the Centrifuge order book.
```
    function requestDeposit(uint256 assets, address owner, uint256 minAmountOut, uint256 deadline)
```

## Summary

The `UserEscrow` smart contract contains a vulnerability that can possibly allow unauthorized users to transfer tokens out of the contract. Specifically, an attacker can exploit this flaw by manipulating the allowances, thus enabling them to bypass the authorization checks present within the `transferOut` function.

## Vulnerability Detail

The `transferOut` function in the `UserEscrow` contract makes use of a conditional check, where if a receiver's allowance, as set in the `token` contract for a given `destination`, equals `type(uint256).max`, then the function will permit the transfer of tokens. # Lines of code

# Vulnerability details

## Impact
An user who is allowed to invest can maliciously drain all the tokens from the ``UserEscrow`` contract from ``decreaseDepositRequest()`` and ``decreaseRedeemRequest()`` of ``LiquidityPool.sol`` contract. Both functions are first send to the router and when the call is returned by the router ``handleExecutedDecreaseInvestOrder()`` and ``handleExecutedDecreaseRedeemorder()`` are executed which both lack necessary checks to verify whether the user has requested deposit/redeem or not. The amount returned by this function to the user is also not verified with the amount send by the user while requesting deposit/redeem.

## Proof of Concept
1. Alice requests a deposit of X amount of currency tokens and those tokens are sent to to the ``UserEscrow`` contract from the ``requestDeposit`` function.
https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-09-centrifuge/blob/512e7a71ebd9ae76384f837204216f26380c9f91/src/InvestmentManager.sol#L136
2. Eve sees this transaction and calls ``decreaseDepositRequest()`` on ``LiquidityPool.sol`` contract to  decrease her deposit of same currency by X amount.
3. Eve steals all the X amount of Alice's currency.

This same attack is also prevalent with ``decreaseRedeemRequest()`` function.

## Tools Used
Manual Analysis

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
In the ``handleExecutedDecreaseInvestOrder()`` and ``handleExecutedDecreaseRedeemorder()``, add the mechanism to do the following things:
1. There is no check to determine whether the user who is requesting decrease deposit/redeem order has deposited previously. This can be tracked using a mapping and should revert user has not deposited.
2. There is no check to verify the amount asked to be decreased is less than or equal to the amount deposited by the user. This should also be tracked and checked.

# Vulnerability details

## Description
The `convertToShares` function calculates the number of shares based on the provided assets and the "latestPrice" obtained from the liquidityPool. While the code may appear straightforward, there is a specific security concern related to divide-by-zero errors in this function.

## Impact
> Divide-by-Zero Risk-> The latestPrice value obtained from the liquidityPool is used as the denominator in a division operation. If, at any point, this latestPrice value becomes zero, it can result in a divide-by-zero error. Such an error would cause the contract to halt, potentially leading to unexpected behavior and disrupting normal operations

## Tools Used
Manual Review

Divide-by-Zero Protection: Before executing the division operation, implement a validation check to ensure that the latestPrice value is non-zero. Utilize a require statement to validate this condition before proceeding with share calculations, as shown below-

```
uint256 latestPrice = LiquidityPoolLike(liquidityPool).latestPrice();
require(latestPrice != 0, "Latest price is zero.");
shares = assets.mulDiv(10 ** (PRICE_DECIMALS + trancheTokenDecimals - currencyDecimals), latestPrice, MathLib.Rounding.Down);

requestDeposit() - Requests a deposit, locks up the assets.

requestDeposit() locks up the assets, but does not mint any shares.

- Attacker receives pool shares for 100 DAI deposit

- So the attacker has spoofed a deposit to get free shares.

Manual

- Tracking deposits and only allowing shares to be collected if there is a corresponding request

- Tracking deposits requested and collected per user, to prevent collecting shares without a deposit.

## Impact
If a user has requested a deposit and lost his member status before the epoch of the RWA pool has ended, there is no way for him to cancel the deposit and since he is no longer on the members list, he will not be able to claim and redeem his tranch tokens. 

## Proof of Concept

Once a user has requested a deposit, the stable coins he wants to invest are send to Escrow.
If he wants to cancel his deposit request, he can either send a new deposit request with 0 and the amount or decrease his deposit by the amount he initially requested. Both options would result in a refund of his stable coins. The issue that arises when the user requests a deposit, loses his member status before the deposit has been executed from the side of centrifuge and tries to cancel his deposit. Both functions `requestDeposit` and `reduceDeposit` check if the user is on the member list of the pool. If he is not the functions will revert and the request to cancel his deposit request will not be processed. This will result in the initial deposit request to be executed. The amount of tranch tokens will be minted to the escrow for the user to redeem. But since he is no longer on the member list, he will not be able to do so and his funds will be lost. 



## Tools Used
Manual review


## Recommended Mitigation Steps

When calling `requestDeposit`, the check if the user is on the member list should only be done when the amount is > 0. If the amount is 0 the request should be processed without the check. This way users that lose their member status will still be able to cancel their deposit request by calling `requestDeposit` with the value of 0.

# Vulnerability details

## Impact
If the root removes itself as ward from contracts like `Gateway`, core update functionalities will not be executable any more

## Proof of Concept
The Root contract is ward for most of the contracts of the protocol and is used to manage the contracts and EOA that are wards for those contracts. This management is done by calling `relyContract` to add wards or `denyContracts` to remove wards. The issue is that in the function `denyContract()` there is no check if the contract to be removed as ward is the Root contract itself. If by any accident the root address is pasted as the contract to be removed as ward, no contract will be left that can manage the wards. For example, if the Root contract removes itself from being ward of the `Gateway` contract, there will not be any option to add or remove incoming routers or update the outgoing router.   

## Tools Used
Manual review


## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Add a check to `Root.denyContract()` to ensure that the user address used as an argument when removing a contract as ward is not the address of the root itself. If it is, make sure that the function reverts.

Access Control

# Vulnerability details

### Impact
A malicious admin can exploit the inherent nature of public blockchain networks to monitor pending transactions. By front-running the `deny` function call, they can execute the `rely` function to grant privileges to another malicious address before their original access is revoked. This can potentially lead to unauthorized access and control over the system's functionalities.

### Proof of Concept
[Link to the code in GitHub](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-09-centrifuge/blob/512e7a71ebd9ae76384f837204216f26380c9f91/src/util/Auth.sol#L20)

### Tools Used
Manual review

### Recommended Mitigation Steps
1. Implement a delay mechanism for administrative actions to provide a window for detecting and countering malicious activities.
2. Use an off-chain multi-signature mechanism for critical administrative functions.
3. Monitor and alert for suspicious admin activities in real-time.

issues.title: Signature Replay Vulnerability in ERC20 `permit` function
issues.body:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-09-centrifuge/blob/512e7a71ebd9ae76384f837204216f26380c9f91/src/token/ERC20.sol#L206


# Vulnerability details

### Impact
The `permit` function in the ERC20 contract uses the native `ecrecover` function to recover the signer's address from the signature. 
Due to the elliptic curve properties, there are two different y-coordinates that correspond to the same x-coordinate. This means that for a given r and s value of a signature, there are two possible public keys that can be recovered. An attacker can potentially exploit this to replay a signature.

### Proof of Concept
[ERC20.sol#L206](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-09-centrifuge/blob/512e7a71ebd9ae76384f837204216f26380c9f91/src/token/ERC20.sol#L206)

### Tools Used
Manual review

### Recommended Mitigation Steps
Replace the native `ecrecover` function with OpenZeppelin's `ECDSA.recover` function to ensure that the signature is correctly validated and to prevent any potential replay attacks.






## Assessed type

Access Control

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-09-centrifuge/blob/main/src/LiquidityPool.sol#L237
https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-09-centrifuge/blob/main/src/LiquidityPool.sol#L295


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
User by exploiting this he can take other users share assets 

## Proof of Concept
The LiquidityPool.transferFrom calls the transferFrom of share token :

```
 function transferFrom(address, address, uint256) public returns (bool) {
        (bool success, bytes memory data) = address(share).call(bytes.concat(msg.data, bytes20(msg.sender)));
        _successCheck(success);
        return abi.decode(data, (bool));
    }
```

the function is public and has no restriction, this can results for the following attack scenario :

userA approves LiquidityPool to spend 500 tokens on share token
userB calls the transferFrom(userA,userB,450)
now the userA will loses his 450 share tokens to userB without his will/intention


## Tools Used
Remix IDE

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
The function should not be called by anyone, at lease a check must be made as the spender is the owner
